scenario: A team stores switch configurations as templates in a Git repository and deploys them with automation. Someone changed a switch by hand at the console. What problem does this create?

options.text: Configuration drift: the device no longer matches the version-controlled source of truth

options.note: That's a switching loop symptom, unrelated to how changes are made.
That's an attack using double tagging or switch spoofing.
That's traffic taking different paths in each direction.

explanation: With infrastructure as code, the repository is the source of truth. Manual changes cause drift that the next automated deployment may overwrite. Changes should go through version control and review.

scenario: A top-of-rack switch needs 40 Gbps uplinks to the spine switches. Which pluggable transceiver form factor is typical?

options.note: SFP supports up to about 1 Gbps.
An RJ45 connector, not a transceiver for 40G uplinks.

explanation: SFP (1G), SFP+ (10G), SFP28 (25G), QSFP+ (40G) and QSFP28 (100G) are common. QSFP stands for quad small form-factor pluggable: four lanes in one module.

scenario: A remote site uses a geostationary satellite link for internet access. Users report that video calls feel delayed even though bandwidth is adequate. What is the main reason?

options.text: High latency from the long round trip to geostationary orbit
Crosstalk between pairs in the cabling
options.note: Crosstalk is a copper cabling issue.
Duplex mismatches cause errors and collisions, not consistently high delay.
That stops new clients from getting addresses.

explanation: Geostationary satellites orbit about 35,786 km up, adding roughly 600 ms or more of round-trip delay. Low Earth orbit (LEO) services reduce latency considerably.

scenario: One router interface connects to a switch trunk carrying VLANs 10, 20 and 30, and the router routes between them. What must you configure on the router?

options.text: A subinterface per VLAN with 802.1Q encapsulation and an IP address for each VLAN
A separate physical interface for each VLAN
options.note: Possible, but this design uses one trunk link.
Routers don't run STP to route between VLANs.

options.text: A native VLAN for each subnet
options.note: There is only one native VLAN per trunk.

explanation: This is "router on a stick": subinterfaces such as g0/0.10 with encapsulation dot1Q 10 act as each VLAN's default gateway. Layer 3 switches use switch virtual interfaces instead.

scenario: Hosts use 10.1.1.1 as their default gateway. Two routers share this address so that hosts keep working if one router fails. What is 10.1.1.1 called?

options.note: Loopbacks are logical interfaces on one device.
The broadcast address reaches every host on a subnet.

explanation: First hop redundancy protocols such as VRRP and HSRP present a virtual IP (and virtual MAC) that moves to the standby router when the active one fails. Hosts never change their gateway.

scenario: A server room's humidity has dropped to 15% in winter. Which risk increases most?

options.note: That's the risk of high humidity.
Humidity doesn't meaningfully change fiber loss.

explanation: Too-dry air increases static buildup and ESD; too-humid air risks condensation and corrosion. Data centers typically keep relative humidity roughly between 40% and 60% and monitor it with environmental sensors.

scenario: A vendor has announced that a firewall model reaches end of support next year. What does this mean for the organization?

options.text: After that date the vendor stops security patches and support, so the device should be replaced before then
The device stops forwarding traffic on that date
options.note: It keeps working, but without fixes.

options.text: The device's warranty is extended automatically
options.note: End of support is the opposite.
Patches and technical support end too.

explanation: End of life (EOL) usually means a product is no longer sold; end of support (EOS) means no more updates or help. Life-cycle management tracks these dates in the asset inventory so replacements are planned and budgeted.

scenario: Old switches are being decommissioned and sent to a recycler. What should happen first?

options.text: Remove them from inventory and monitoring, and securely erase their configurations, which can contain credentials and keys
Ship them as they are, since switches don't store data
options.note: Configs can include passwords, SNMP strings and keys.

options.text: Just unplug the power so the running config is lost
options.note: The startup config is still saved in NVRAM.

options.text: Leave them in the monitoring system for history
options.note: Stale entries cause false alerts and clutter.

explanation: Decommissioning follows a documented process: back up and erase configurations (or destroy storage), update asset records, IPAM, diagrams and monitoring, and keep chain-of-custody records for disposal.

scenario: An SNMP manager needs to read the inbound error counter of a specific switch interface. What identifies that value in the device's data structure?

options.text: An object identifier (OID) defined in a MIB

options.note: Community strings are SNMPv1/v2c passwords, not data identifiers.
SNMP uses UDP 161 for queries; ports don't identify values.
Severity is part of syslog messages, not SNMP.

explanation: A management information base (MIB) describes the values a device exposes. Each value has a numeric OID, such as the ifInErrors counter for an interface. Managers poll OIDs; agents send traps for events (UDP 162).

scenario: You need to know which hosts talk to which, on what ports, and how much data they send, across a WAN link for capacity planning, without capturing full packets. What should you collect?

options.text: Flow data such as NetFlow, IPFIX or sFlow
Full packet captures on every link
options.note: Possible, but storage-heavy and more than you need.
Counters show totals per interface, not who talks to whom.
Syslog records events, not traffic conversations.

explanation: Flow records summarize conversations (source, destination, ports, protocol, bytes, packets) and are exported to a collector for traffic analysis. Packet capture is for deep inspection of specific problems.

scenario: A company wants a disaster recovery site with power, network links and some equipment already in place, ready to run within a day or two after restoring recent backups. Which type of site is this?

options.note: A hot site is fully equipped and replicated, ready almost immediately, at higher cost.
A cold site has space and power but little or no equipment.
A tabletop is an exercise, not a facility.

explanation: Cold, warm and hot sites trade cost against recovery time. Choose the site type that meets the recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO) at an acceptable cost.

scenario: Security wants clients to verify that the time they receive from NTP servers is authentic and hasn't been tampered with. What should be deployed?

options.note: DNSSEC protects DNS answers, not time.
PTP improves precision; NTS adds authentication to NTP.
SNMPv3 secures management traffic, not time sync.

explanation: NTS uses TLS for key establishment, then authenticates NTP packets, protecting against spoofed time. Accurate time matters for logs, certificates and Kerberos.

scenario: An attacker follows an employee through a badge-controlled door before it closes. What is this called, and what control best prevents it?

options.text: Tailgating, prevented by an access control vestibule (mantrap)
Shoulder surfing, prevented by privacy screens
options.note: Shoulder surfing is watching someone enter information.
That's searching the trash for information.

explanation: Tailgating (or piggybacking, when the employee knowingly lets them in) defeats badge readers. Access control vestibules, security guards, turnstiles and staff training reduce it.

scenario: Printed network diagrams and old password lists are thrown in a dumpster behind the office. Which attack does this enable, and what control prevents it?

options.text: Dumpster diving, prevented by shredding and secure disposal policies

options.note: An evil twin is a rogue access point.

options.text: ARP poisoning, prevented by dynamic ARP inspection
VLAN hopping, prevented by disabling DTP

explanation: Social engineers search trash for useful information. Shred sensitive documents, use locked disposal bins, and include media destruction in data handling policies.

scenario: Many network devices use SSH keys, TLS certificates and SNMPv3 credentials. Which practice reduces the risk of a compromised or expired key causing an outage or breach?

options.text: Key management: generate keys securely, store them protected, track expiry, rotate them and revoke them when compromised
Use the same key on every device to simplify renewal
options.note: One leaked key would compromise everything.
That exposes credentials in clear text.

options.text: Keep private keys in the network diagram documentation
options.note: Private keys must never be stored in shared documents.

explanation: Key management covers the whole life cycle of cryptographic keys and certificates. Inventory them, alert before expiry, rotate regularly, and revoke compromised keys and certificates promptly.

scenario: Customer payment card data must be stored and processed only in data centers inside the European Union. Which concept does this describe?

options.note: Geofencing triggers actions based on a device's location.
Least privilege limits access rights, not where data lives.

explanation: Regulations such as GDPR and contracts can require data to stay in specific jurisdictions. Network and cloud designs must keep data, and often backups and replicas, in approved regions.

scenario: You need to discover which hosts are up on 10.20.0.0/24 and which TCP ports they have open, to compare with your documentation. Which tool should you use?

options.note: It shows the path to one destination.
It shows the local host's IP settings.

explanation: Nmap scans for live hosts, open ports, services and OS fingerprints. Only scan networks you're authorized to test, because scanning can trigger security alerts.

scenario: Laptops keep dropping their Wi-Fi connection briefly and reconnecting, mostly in one part of the building. Signal there is weak. What is the most likely issue?

options.text: Insufficient coverage causing client disassociation; add or reposition access points after a site survey
A DHCP lease time that is too long
A duplex mismatch on the AP uplink
options.note: That causes slow wired performance for all clients, not location-specific drops.

options.text: An expired SSL certificate on the web server

explanation: Weak signal and interference make clients disassociate and reassociate. Wireless surveys and heat maps show coverage gaps. Fixes include adding APs, adjusting placement, power and channels, and checking roaming settings.

scenario: After the troubleshooting team implements a fix for an outage, what should they do next, according to the CompTIA methodology?

options.text: Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures
Establish a theory of probable cause
options.note: That comes before testing and implementing a fix.

options.text: Close the ticket immediately without testing
options.note: Verification comes before documentation and closure.

explanation: The steps are: identify the problem; establish a theory of probable cause; test the theory; establish a plan of action and identify potential effects; implement the solution or escalate; verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures; document findings, actions, outcomes and lessons learned.

scenario: A switch port connected to a new access point is up, but the AP keeps rebooting. The switch's show power inline output shows the port is denied power. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The switch's PoE power budget is exhausted, or the AP needs more power than the port's PoE standard provides
The VLAN on the port is wrong
options.note: A wrong VLAN affects connectivity, not power.
Plenum rating concerns fire safety, not power.

explanation: PoE (802.3af, about 15.4 W), PoE+ (802.3at, about 30 W) and PoE++ (802.3bt, up to about 90 W) differ in available power. Check the device's requirement, the per-port standard and the total budget on the switch.
